## Effects the FY2023 10-K attributes to the war in Ukraine and the resulting sanctions/export controls

**1. Access to markets was blocked.** In Item 1A (Risk Factors, p. 28), NVIDIA's own example of the sanctions/export-control regime states:

> "in response to the war in Ukraine, the United States and other jurisdictions imposed economic sanctions and export control measures which blocked the passage of our products, services and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine."

So the stated effects were (a) blockage of products, (b) blockage of services, and (c) blockage of support — into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine.

**2. Direct sales to Russia were stopped and Russian operations were closed.** Item 1A (p. 28): "In fiscal year 2023, we stopped direct sales to Russia and closed business operations in Russia." MD&A, "Russia" (p. 37) gives the same facts with sequencing: "In fiscal year 2023, we stopped direct sales to Russia and later in the year, we closed business operations in Russia." MD&A also adds the counterpoint that "Direct sales to Russia in fiscal year 2022 were immaterial," i.e., the exit did not come at the cost of a material direct-sales revenue stream.

**3. Sales to partners who sell into Russia may have been negatively affected.** MD&A (p. 37): "Our revenue to partners that sell into Russia may have been negatively impacted due to the war in Ukraine." (Hedged as possibly having occurred, so it qualifies as a described effect, not a future-only risk.)

**4. End-customer sales in EMEA were affected by the war itself.** Item 1A (p. 28): "Concurrently, the war in Ukraine has impacted end customer sales in EMEA and may continue to do so in the future."

**5. Related export-license measures already in force that also cover Russia.** Item 1 "Government Regulations" (p. 11) and Item 1A (p. 29) and MD&A "Global Trade" (p. 37) describe the Q3 FY2023 U.S. rules:

> "During the third quarter of fiscal year 2023, the U.S. government announced new license requirements that impact certain exports to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and Russia of some of our data center products. The impact of the new license requirements is difficult to quantify, and it may be challenging for us to manage our operations and forecast our operating results due to these requirements."

Specifically, the licensing requirements "impact our A100 and H100 integrated circuits, DGX or any other systems or boards which incorporate A100 or H100 integrated circuits and our A100X," and extend to "any future NVIDIA integrated circuit achieving certain peak performance and chip-to-chip I/O performance thresholds." In addition, NVIDIA "are required to transition certain operations out of China (including Hong Kong), including research and development and supply and distribution operations," which "could be costly and time consuming, and adversely affect our research and development and supply and distribution operations, as well as our revenue, during any such transition period." NVIDIA also engaged with China customers to offer alternatives not subject to the license requirements (e.g., the A800).

**6. Materiality caveat stated by the filing.** Item 1 (p. 11): "Compliance with laws, rules, and regulations has not otherwise had a material effect upon our capital expenditures, results of operations, or competitive position." Note also that the filing's revenue-by-geography table (Note 17, p. 85) reports only U.S., Taiwan, China (incl. Hong Kong), and "Other countries" — Russia is not separately disclosed — and the fiscal 2023 decline in revenue outside the U.S. (84% to 69%) is attributed to China and Taiwan, not to Russia/Ukraine. The $2.17 billion fiscal 2023 inventory provision and gross-margin decline are likewise attributed to China demand expectations, not to Ukraine.

## Excluded as future-only risks
The filing's forward-looking sanctions/export-control risks are not treated as having occurred: additional or broader unilateral/multilateral export controls on AI products; retaliatory measures by foreign governments (including China) affecting NVIDIA's supply chain or worldwide product sales; license delays, denials, or temporary/burdensome license conditions; customers shifting to competitors or to China-, Europe-, or Israel-based semiconductor suppliers; pre-/post-sale technical support becoming more cumbersome and less certain; excess inventory if alternative offerings cannot be sold in China; increased use of economic sanctions reducing demand; penalties for violations of export control or sanctions laws; and heightened cyber-attack risk "during times of war." The filing also notes only that the war "may continue" to affect EMEA end-customer sales in the future.

### Headline

Gross margin increased to **75.0% in fiscal 2025** from **72.7% in fiscal 2024** (up 2.3 percentage points), with cost of revenue falling from 27.3% to 25.0% of revenue. NVIDIA states the increase "was primarily driven by a higher mix of Data Center revenue." The 10-K does **not** provide a full quantitative gross-margin bridge; it identifies the factors qualitatively plus the one quantified item (inventory).

### Favorable factors

1. **Higher mix of Data Center revenue.** This is the stated primary driver. Data Center revenue rose 142% year over year on demand for the Hopper platform, and Compute & Networking segment revenue rose 145% to $116.2 billion, versus Graphics revenue growth of only 6% (to $14.3 billion). Because Data Center/platform revenue carries a higher margin than Gaming/Graphics, the shift in revenue mix lifted consolidated gross margin.

2. **Smaller net drag from inventory provisions than in fiscal 2024.** Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $3.7 billion in fiscal 2025 versus $2.2 billion in fiscal 2024, but provision releases from sales of previously reserved inventory and settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations were $689 million in fiscal 2025 versus $540 million in fiscal 2024. The **net effect on gross margin was an unfavorable impact of 2.3% in fiscal 2025, compared with 2.7% in fiscal 2024** — i.e., the year-over-year change in this item was itself a modest favorable contributor.

3. **Slightly lower acquisition-related intangible amortization.** Cost of revenue includes acquisition-related intangible amortization expense; amortization expense was $593 million in fiscal 2025 versus $614 million in fiscal 2024 (Note 6).

1. **Inventory provisions and excess inventory purchase obligations (the dominant unfavorable item).** These charges are recorded in cost of revenue and were the principal drag on gross margin in fiscal 2025:
   - Inventory provision: **$1.6 billion** in fiscal 2025 versus $774 million in fiscal 2024 (Note 9).
   - Excess inventory purchase obligations expense: **approximately $2.0 billion** in fiscal 2025 versus $1.4 billion in fiscal 2024 (Note 9); the excess inventory purchase obligation balance rose to $2.095 billion from $1.655 billion.
   
   The 10-K attributes these provisions to situations that "may result in excess or obsolete inventory or excess product purchase commitments," including changes in business and economic conditions, sudden and significant decreases in demand, inventory obsolescence from changing technology, new product introductions reducing demand for existing products, failure to estimate customer demand properly, ordering in advance of historical lead times, and regulatory impacts. These are largely driven by the accelerated Blackwell/annual product cadence, long manufacturing lead times (in some cases extending beyond twelve months), and non-cancellable orders placed in advance of historical lead times with premiums and deposits paid to secure supply and capacity.

2. **Stock-based compensation in cost of revenue rose.** Cost of revenue stock-based compensation was **$178 million** in fiscal 2025 versus $141 million in fiscal 2024 (Note 3), reflecting employee growth and compensation increases. (Total company stock-based compensation was $4.737 billion vs. $3.549 billion, but the vast majority sits in R&D and SG&A, not cost of revenue.)

3. **Rising product warranty and return provisions.** Product warranty and return provisions in accrued liabilities grew to **$1.373 billion** from $415 million, and accrued product warranty liabilities reached $1.3 billion versus $306 million a year earlier, with recent additions primarily from Compute & Networking (Note 9, Note 12). Warranty provisions are estimated and recorded in cost of revenue.

4. **Macroeconomic and cost pressures.** The 10-K notes that macroeconomic factors — inflation, interest rate changes, capital market volatility, global supply chain constraints, **tariffs**, and global economic and geopolitical developments — "may have direct and indirect impacts on our results of operations," affecting supply chain and manufacturing costs, employee wages, and costs for capital equipment. **Source:** Pfizer Inc. 2024 Form 10-K (filed Feb. 27, 2025) — MD&A "Analysis of the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows" (p. 46 of the filing), the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows (p. 55), Note 1I, Note 2A, Note 8A and Note 17C.

### The 10-K's stated cause

Operating activities provided **$12,744 million in 2024 vs. $8,700 million in 2023** (and $29,267 million in 2022). Pfizer states in MD&A:

> "The change was driven primarily by an increase in net income adjusted for non-cash items, partially offset by the timing of receipts and payments in the ordinary course of business, including a decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid and net changes in inventory greater than one year (see Note 8A)."

So there is one positive driver and three stated offsets: (a) the timing of receipts and payments in the ordinary course of business; (b) the decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid; and (c) net changes in inventory greater than one year.

### The positive driver: higher net income adjusted for non-cash items

- Net income from continuing operations before allocation to noncontrolling interests rose from **$2,172 million to $8,051 million**. The MD&A attributes the $7.0 billion increase in pretax income from continuing operations to (i) a decrease in cost of sales, (ii) higher revenues and (iii) a decrease in restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs, partly offset by (iv) higher net interest expense, (v) net periodic benefit costs on pension/postretirement plans in 2024 versus net credits in 2023, (vi) lower net gains on equity securities and (vii) higher intangible amortization.
- Cost of sales fell **$7.1 billion**, mainly the **non-recurrence of the 2023 non-cash COVID-19 inventory write-off charge of $6.2 billion** ($5.0 billion Paxlovid and $1.2 billion Comirnaty) plus a **$2.6 billion favorable sales mix**, partly offset by a **$1.9 billion Seagen impact, inclusive of amortization of the fair value step-up of inventory**. Revenue rose $4.1 billion (7%) to $63.6 billion on Paxlovid, a full year of legacy Seagen, Vyndaqel and Eliquis, partly offset by Comirnaty declines and foreign exchange.
- Quantitatively, net income plus non-cash adjustments rose from about **$10.9 billion in 2023 to about $15.8 billion in 2024** (+$4.9 billion): depreciation and amortization $7,013 vs. $6,290; asset write-offs and impairments $4,242 vs. $3,408; share-based compensation $877 vs. $525; deferred taxes $(2,102) vs. $(3,442); benefit-plan contributions in excess of expense $(12) vs. $(787); **COVID-19 inventory write-offs $0 vs. $6,199**; other adjustments, net $(2,260) vs. $(3,492). Note that the disappearance of the $6.2 billion COVID-19 write-off add-back in 2024 largely offset the earnings recovery in cash terms, since those2023 charges were non-cash.

### Offsetting factors

1. **Timing of receipts and payments in the ordinary course of business.** Total working-capital changes were a **$3,066 million use of cash in 2024 versus $2,172 million in 2023** (a $0.9 billion larger drag): inventories $(854) vs. $(1,169); trade accounts receivable $(109) vs. $347; other assets $3,380 vs. $(663); trade accounts payable $(1,023) vs. $(300); **other liabilities $(3,115) vs. $595**; other tax accounts, net $(1,345) vs. $(982).
2. **Decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid.** Paxlovid and Comirnaty deferred revenues fell from **$5.1 billion at December 31, 2023 to $2.2 billion at December 31, 2024** (current $1.4 billion; noncurrent $785 million), primarily because amounts were recognized in product revenues as products were delivered (including $442 million from the one-time contractual delivery of Paxlovid treatment courses to the U.S. SNS) and the $771 million favorable final Paxlovid adjustment recorded in Q1 2024, partly offset by new advance payments under amended contracts. Approximately **$2.9 billion** of the year-end 2023 deferred revenue balance was recognized as revenue in 2024. This drawdown of customer prepayments is a use of operating cash flow.
3. **Net changes in inventory greater than one year** (see below).

### The change in inventories not expected to be sold within one year

Under its accounting policy (Note 1I), Pfizer classifies inventories not expected to be sold within 12 months as **Other noncurrent assets** (Note 8A). These **noncurrent inventories fell from $4,568 million at December 31, 2023 to $2,663 million at December 31, 2024**, a decrease of about $1.9 billion.

**The cause Pfizer gives:** "The decrease from December 31, 2023 is **primarily driven by a reduction in acquired Seagen inventory, inclusive of the acquisition accounting fair value step up**" (Note 8A, referencing Note 2A). Pfizer adds: "Based on our current estimates and assumptions, there are **no recoverability issues** for these amounts."

Supporting context from Note 2A: in the final purchase-price allocation for Seagen (acquired December 14, 2023), inventories were recognized at fair value of **$3,273 million as adjusted (after a $(922) million measurement-period adjustment), comprising $1.1 billion of current inventories and $2.1 billion of noncurrent inventories**. As those acquired inventories were sold during 2024, the acquisition-accounting fair value step-up was amortized through Cost of sales — the MD&A's $1.9 billion Seagen impact on 2024 cost of sales is "inclusive of the amortization of the fair value step-up of inventory" — reducing the noncurrent inventory balance without a corresponding cash outflow.

**The offsetting inventory movement:** current inventories (those expected to be sold within a year) **rose from $10,189 million to $10,851 million**, which Pfizer attributes to "higher inventory levels for certain products mainly due to changes in net market demand, network strategy and new product launches." (Finished goods $3,495 → $3,775; work-in-process $5,688 → $6,101; raw materials and supplies $1,007 → $976.) For prior-year context, the 2023 Form 10-K's Note 8A explained the then $1.3 billion decline in noncurrent inventories as driven by Paxlovid write-offs of $4.2 billion and, to a lesser extent, Comirnaty write-offs of $0.7 billion, offset by roughly $3.1 billion of acquired Seagen inventory including the fair value step-up.

### Summary

The $4.0 billion increase in operating cash flow is attributed primarily to higher net income adjusted for non-cash items (reflecting the 2023 non-recurrence of $6.2 billion of COVID-19 inventory write-offs and charges, higher 2024 revenues and lower cost of sales, partly offset by Seagen's $1.9 billion cost impact and higher interest expense, amortization and lower equity-security gains), and is partially offset by ordinary-course timing of receipts and payments — notably the drawdown of Comirnaty and Paxlovid advance payments/deferred revenues (from $5.1 billion to $2.2 billion) and the net change in noncurrent inventories, whose $1.9 billion decline Pfizer attributes to the run-off of acquired Seagen inventory including its acquisition-accounting fair value step-up, with no recoverability issues.
